body.objective: Students will be able to tune with a tuner and by ear.
body.iCan: I can tune with a tuner and by ear.
successCriteria: I can use a tuner to check my pitch
I can adjust my instrument when sharp or flat
I can hear beats and tune by ear
body.hook: Two instruments almost in tune create a "wah-wah" wobble called beats. When they match perfectly, the wobble disappears and the sound becomes one. Tuning is training your ears to hear that.

vocabulary.definition: How accurately in tune a player is.
A device that shows whether a note is sharp, flat or in tune.
Small units of pitch on a tuner; 100 cents = one half step.
A wobbling sound when two pitches are close but not matched.

study.title: In Tune Together
study.question: How do I tune my instrument?
study.passage:
Tuning guide (written for this lesson):
1. Warm up first; cold instruments play flat.
2. Tuning note: usually Concert B♭ (or Concert A for some groups).
3. Tuner: play a steady mf note; read the needle. Within about ±5 cents is close.
4. Adjust: If sharp (too high), lengthen the instrument: pull out the tuning slide, headjoint, barrel or mouthpiece. If flat (too low), shorten it: push in. Make small changes.
5. By ear: play with a partner or a drone; listen for beats. Faster beats = further apart; beats slow down as you get closer; no beats = in tune.
6. Playing habits also affect pitch: loud playing can go sharp on some instruments; soft playing can go flat; keep air supported.
Mallet percussion and piano are fixed pitch, so percussionists help by playing the reference pitch and listening.

body.objective: Students will be able to balance with my section and the band.
body.iCan: I can balance with my section and the band.
successCriteria: I can explain balance in an ensemble
I can adjust my volume to balance with my section and the band
I can bring out the melody and support it
body.hook: A band where the trumpets drown out everyone sounds like a trumpet solo with background noise. Balance is about every part being heard at the right level, so the music makes sense.

vocabulary.definition: The right volume relationship between parts so everything important is heard.
A second tune played at the same time as the melody.
A balance model where low instruments are strongest and high instruments lighter.
Players in one section matching each other's volume.

study.title: Balanced Band
study.question: How do bands balance their sound?
study.passage:
Balance activities (written for this lesson):
1. Pyramid of sound: play a Concert B♭ chord. Basses (tuba, bass clarinet, baritone sax, bassoon) play the strongest; tenors (trombone, euphonium, horn, tenor sax) a bit less; altos and sopranos (trumpet, clarinet, alto sax, flute, oboe) lightest. Compare with an upside-down pyramid.
2. Section balance: within a section, no single player stands out; if you hear only yourself, come down.
3. Melody up: in a chorale, the conductor names who has the melody; that section plays mf; others play mp. Switch melodies.
4. Countermelody: identify a passage where two tunes happen together; balance them so both are heard.
5. Listening seats: two students go to the back of the room and report what they hear clearly and what's buried.
6. Pencil: mark "MEL" over melody passages and "acc" over accompaniment in your part.

body.objective: Students will be able to blend my sound.
successCriteria: I can match my tone with players around me
I can adjust tone colour, vibrato and attack to blend
I can describe the difference between balance and blend
body.hook: A great section sounds like one giant instrument. Blend is when individual voices disappear into a unified sound, like many voices in a choir singing as one.

vocabulary.definition: Individual sounds merging into one unified sound.
The quality that makes each instrument or player sound different.
Copying the tone, length and style of players around you.
A slight regular wavering of pitch used for expression.
The section leader whose sound others match.

study.title: One Sound
study.question: How does a section blend into one sound?
study.passage:
Blend activities (written for this lesson):
Balance vs blend: balance is about volume between parts; blend is about tone matching so voices merge.
1. Unison test: a section plays Concert F together. Can you pick out individual players? If yes, adjust.
2. Match the lead: the lead player plays a note; the next player matches tone, volume and length; then the next joins, until the whole section plays.
3. Tone colour: play one note bright (open, more edge) and one dark (rounder, warmer). The band chooses one colour for a chorale and everyone matches.
4. Attacks and releases: match how you start ("too" vs "doo") and when you stop.
5. Vibrato: in a young band, usually play without vibrato in unisons unless the lead player uses it; mismatched vibrato stops blend.
6. Cross-section blend: clarinets and flutes play the melody together; adjust until they sound like one new colour.

Choose and match a tone colour
discussion: Could you pick out individuals in the unison test?
